title: Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon Reportedly Backs CLARITY Act In Split From JPMorgan’s Jamie Dimon - TradingView
content: Goldman Sachs Group, Inc (GS) CEO David Solomon said on Thursday that he supported the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act, commonly known as the CLARITY Act, a position that differs from other big bank CEOs, including JPMorgan Chase’s Jamie Dimon, who have opposed the bill. "I'm very supportive of moving the Clarity Act forward, so we can get some market structure in place and start to move the innovation process along," Solomon told POLITICO in an interview. Solomon refused to comment on the views of other bankers, but drew a clear line under Goldman's position. “We believe strongly that we need one system where everybody can participate,” he said, adding that Goldman Sachs’s position is that there will be other things that are “gonna have to happen as we go forward. But it’s a step in the right direction.” Unlike commercial lenders, investment banks like Goldman Sachs rely less on consumer deposits. Solomon said he has been focused on provisions that would allow “institutions that have been on the sidelines to participate more actively,” instead describing that as “the most important thing” in the bill at this stage. GS stock fell over 2% during midday trading. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment around GS remained in the ‘neutral’ zone, while chatter around it stayed at ‘low’ levels over the past day. Solomon spoke just after Senate Republicans began circulating a new text of the bill before a possible floor vote next week. The new text followed an updated draft that Senator Cynthia Lummis (R-WY) unveiled on Wednesday, combining the separate bills previously passed by the Senate Banking and Agriculture Committees. A coalition of the industry’s most powerful groups, including the American Bankers Association (ABA), Bank Policy Institute, and Consumer Bankers Association, also warned on Wednesday that the bill’s stablecoin provision threatens “local lending that drives economic activity in the US at risk.” Solomon’s support puts him at odds with Jamie Dimon, CEO of JPMorgan & Chase (JPM), who had said the legislation would have exposed consumer banks to risk by giving crypto firms an unfair advantage with yield-based rewards on dollar-pegged stablecoins. Dimon also clashed publicly with Coinbase (COIN) CEO Brian Armstrong over the bill’s lobbying push in May. The bill's path forward remains uncertain, with unresolved fights over stablecoins, opposition from law enforcement groups, and the ethics language itself still in play ahead of any Senate vote. Warren Says Crypto Bill Could Never Be Enforced Against Trump Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) argued on Wednesday that the bill's enforcement was ineffective against President Trump himself. It will stop state attorneys general or anyone else from enforcing the law, leaving enforcement solely to Trump's own Attorney General. This meant it would cut off authority entirely once Trump left office, meaning no future Department of Justice (DOJ) could hold him accountable for violations committed while in power. Circle (CRCL) and Coinbase (COIN), the two firms that would benefit most from the CLARITY Act, were down over 5% and 2%, respectively, amid broader market weakness. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around CRCL remained in the ‘bearish’ zone, while retail sentiment around COIN remained in the ‘bullish’ zone. Select market data provided by ICE Data Services. Momentum investing is all about the idea of following a stock's recent trend, which can be in either direction. In the "long context," investors will essentially be "buying high, but hoping to sell even higher." And for investors following this methodology, taking advantage of trends in a stock's price is key; once a stock establishes a course, it is more than likely to continue moving in that direction. The goal is that once a stock heads down a fixed path, it will lead to timely and profitable trades. Even though momentum is a popular stock characteristic, it can be tough to define. Debate surrounding which are the best and worst metrics to focus on is lengthy, but the Zacks Momentum Style Score, part of the Zacks Style Scores, helps address this issue for us. Below, we take a look at Goldman Sachs (GS), a company that currently holds a Momentum Style Score of A. We also talk about price change and earnings estimate revisions, two of the main aspects of the Momentum Style Score. Looking at a stock's short-term price activity is a great way to gauge if it has momentum, since this can reflect both the current interest in a stock and if buyers or sellers have the upper hand at the moment. Over the past quarter, shares of Goldman Sachs have risen 21.27%, and are up 53.06% in the last year. On the other hand, the S&P 500 has only moved 5.37% and 20.16%, respectively. Investors should also take note of GS's average 20-day trading volume. Volume is a useful item in many ways, and the 20-day average establishes a good price-to-volume baseline; a rising stock with above average volume is generally a bullish sign, whereas a declining stock on above average volume is typically bearish. Right now GS is averaging 1,972,181 shares for the last 20 days.. The Zacks Momentum Style Score also takes into account trends in estimate revisions, in addition to price changes. Please note that estimate revision trends remain at the core of Zacks Rank as well. A nice path here can help show promise, and we have recently been seeing that with GS. Over the past two months, 7 earnings estimates moved higher compared to none lower for the full year. These revisions helped boost GS's consensus estimate, increasing from $59.53 to $68.83 in the past 60 days. Looking at the next fiscal year, 7 estimates have moved upwards while there have been no downward revisions in the same time period. Taking into account all of these elements, it should come as no surprise that GS is a #1 (Strong Buy) stock with a Momentum Score of A. The joint venture was established to help agencies access an agile, mission-focused partner with the scale, technical depth and procurement flexibility needed to compete for and execute increasingly complex federal technology programs. “At By Light, we thrive on finding small businesses that complement our own capabilities and combining forces to solve some of the federal government’s most complex technology challenges,” said John Kilpatrick, vice president of space operations at By Light. “With their strength of experience in areas like network engineering and infrastructure, Copper River was a natural fit.” Copper Lights was formed under the U.S. Small Business Administration’s mentor-protégé program, with By Light serving as mentor and Copper River GS serving as protégé. Copper Lights combines By Light’ capabilities in cyber, communications, infrastructure, simulation and mission training with Copper River GS’ experience delivering cybersecurity, enterprise networks, mobility and end-to-end IT solutions. title: The Best Lexus 5.0 V8-Powered Sports Sedan Can Be Yours For The Same Price As A New ES Hybrid - CarBuzz
content: The BMW M5 is one of the most legendary performance cars ever produced, as it revolutionized the executive sports sedan market when it first hit the market in 1985. It has had to deal with a swarm of rivals trying to cash in on the lucrative sector since, though BMWs M Division has continually moved the bar ever higher to ensure the M5 retains its crown as the king of the mid-size premium sports sedan. This doesn't mean other rivals haven't gotten close, or surpassed the M5 in certain respects. The car in question went out of production in 2020, but this only means you can secure one for a lot less than its original MSRP on the used market. In fact, if you're in the market for a Lexus ES, but don't find it spicy enough, this might be the perfect solution. For most of its early history, Lexus tended to focus on the luxury aspect of its vehicles, rather than the sporting side. Some models, like the SC300 coupe, were a little more performative in nature, but they still angled more toward the smooth and silky side of the coin. Looking to expand its customer base, Lexus decided to establish its very own performance arm, called F, in 2006. The F department took a two-pronged approach to jazzing up Lexus' cars. It developed a range of F-Sport trim lines for lower-end models, which brought along mildly hot aesthetic and engineering enhancements, though the full-fat F cars were the ones for the true gearheads. These featured powerful naturally aspirated V8 engines, and focused chassis tuning that ensured they could take the fight to cars made by BMW's M division and Mercedes-Benz's AMG department. While the Lexus IS F was released in 2007 to take on the BMW M3 and Mercedes C63, it took until 2015 before Lexus unveiled a challenger to the likes of the M5. Wanting to be seen as a serious option alongside the mighty M5, Lexus pulled out all the stops to ensure the GS F could battle its German rival in its own backyard. Unfortunately, the GS F was short-lived, as it died along with the rest of the GS lineup after Lexus decided to retire the model in 2020. As a result, the only way to get one now is by purchasing a used example. Given its position as a range-topping executive sports sedan, the GS F wasn't exactly affordable when it was new. Even without any options selected, the GS F demanded over $85,000 from its buyer's bank account. It must be said that this was nearly $20,000 less than the M5's $102,000 price tag in 2020. As is usually the case with expensive vehicles that suffer steep depreciation, the value of the GS F have taken a tumble since then. The CarBuzz Marketplace values a solid 2020 example at $59,457. Earlier model-year cars can be had for significantly less. Bear in mind that the pre-2017 MY GS Fs didn't come with the marque's Adaptive Variable Suspension system, which is well worth having. It uses sensors to monitor the kind of road surface the GS F is traveling over, which can then select one of 30 different damper settings to suit. This ensures that whether the car is attacking a corner on a track or dealing with a rough road, which requires a smoother ride, it can change at a moment's notice. Prices for earlier models range vastly. A first model year with 100,000 miles on the clock can go for as little as $38,000, while a 2018 model with 30,000 miles of wear and tear will retail for $45,000. A good price to keep in mind is $50,000. For that, you get a car with the Adaptive Variable Suspension in one of the GS F's more sedate colors. For those looking for outright pace over a purely thrilling driving experience, it'll be difficult to see past the M5. The F90 version of the model introduced in 2018 comes with a 4.4-liter twin-turbo V8 packing 600 hp, which thoroughly decimates the 467 hp naturally aspirated V8 found under the hood of the GS F. As a result, while the M5 can hit 60 mph in a blazing 3.2 seconds, the GS F gets there in 4.5 seconds. Both come with automatic eight-speed transmissions. That said, the Lexus' V8 offers a much more exciting sound than the rather muted tones of the M5's twin-turbo unit, making it feel a little more alive when you hit the throttle. The GS F is also rear-wheel-drive as opposed to the all-wheel-drive BMW, which helps ensure the Lexus tips the scales at around 300 pounds less. For those looking to get their pulse racing, these rawer elements may prove more appealing than the efficiently quick M5. We wouldn't call one driving experience better than the other. They go about it in different ways as mentioned earlier. The F90 M5 has AWD because it needs it. 600 horses is just too much for the real world, especially in wet conditions. The GS F is a more balanced experience, and the 467 hp V8 never feels like more than the chassis (or driver) can cope with. You also can't beat the immediacy of a naturally aspirated V8 engine, which is all but gone from the new automotive market. In the case of the GS F, you're buying an experience that's no longer available. Even its little brother is no longer on sale, and as a result, its value have gone through the roof. While both share Lexus’ glorious, high-revving 5.0-liter naturally aspirated V8, the GS F stands out as a purpose-built performance machine, whereas the IS 500 is essentially a standard sport sedan with a huge engine shoehorned inside. As a true "F" model, the GS F gets extensive chassis bracing, massive six-piston Brembo brakes, and a sophisticated Torque Vectoring Differential for exceptional track handling. In contrast, the IS 500 carries base IS 350 brakes and a basic Torsen limited-slip differential. Add in aggressive sport seats, a roomier cabin, and superior cooling, and the GS F emerges as an uncompromised future classic. Aside from providing a thrilling drive, the GS F can also be trusted to get you to your next destination. While this shouldn't come as much of a surprise given Lexus' reputation for bulletproof reliability, as illustrated by the brand winning several JD Power dependability surveys in a row. RepairPal estimates the V8-powered beast should only cost around $499 a year to maintain. Its strong performance continues when you consider the National Highway Transport Safety Administration's records. The US Government-run department, which ensures every car sold in the US is safe, has yet to receive a single complaint regarding the car from an owner. One recall was filed for the vehicle by Lexus, which concerned the high-pressure fuel pump fitted to certain GS Fs made between 2016 and 2018. The component's cover could crack under load, which risked leading to a fire. All vehicles affected should already have had the fuel pump replacement carried out, but make sure when looking at a used example to confirm this. All in all, the GS F positions itself as a worthy alternative not just to the M5, but also to any new Lexus sedan. The 2026 Lexus IS starts at $46,895 and only offers an old-school V6. The all-new ES Hybrid starts at $51,095, and while it will undoubtedly be more modern, sophisticated, and frugal, all you'll get at this price point is a 244-hp four-cylinder hybrid. title: Four petrol bikes and one electric: Dalmatia, Bosnia, 3,000+ kilometers – How does that work? - THE PACK – Electric motorcycle news
content: First of all, a note of thanks: huge thanks to Manfred Janek for generously sharing this story, and to SteckerBiker for making the connection. These real-life, real-mileage travel reports are exactly the kind of content THE PACK wants more of: honest, funny, unglamorous-in-the-best-way accounts of what it’s actually like to ride electric, day after day, alongside people who didn’t necessarily choose to believe in it yet. (Story and photos originally by Manfred Janek for SteckerBiker. English retelling for THE PACK, based on the original German article >). Manfred Janek is now in his third season riding electric, and each year the concept wins him over a little more. His riding group runs a big annual tour, and in past years he’d simply retraced their petrol-bike routes afterward on his electric bike, solo – first a four-day loop through Bavaria and Austria, then a demanding 2,500 km, eight-day, roughly 30-pass run combining the Route des Grandes Alpes with Tuscany. For 2026, there was nothing left to retrace. So he decided to just join the group ride itself … on the electric bike. That meant matching pace with four full-size combustion machines: a BMW R1300 GS, a BMW R 1250 GS, a BMW F 750 GS, and a Ducati Multistrada V4S. Complicating things further, the whole route had already been planned by the R 1300 GS rider, hotels booked and daily stages fixed, back when everyone assumed Manfred would be riding his usual BMW K 1200 R. His first tentative suggestion of bringing the electric bike instead was flatly rejected. Only after checking that the route avoided highways and had just one stage over 400 km did the group come around. Manfred then built his own parallel plan: a charging point for every lunch stop, overnight charging at hotels, and – since the Großglockner pass was still on his personal electric-bike bucket list – a two-day solo extension after the group split off in Bosnia. He also had to switch hotels in Sarajevo when the original one couldn’t offer charging. That left him the outsider on three counts: electric instead of petrol, a solo cabin on the night train instead of sharing a four-berth compartment with the others, and a different hotel in Sarajevo. Not exactly the ingredients for a harmonious group photo. Manfred: “What you won’t find here, however, are elaborate descriptions of landscapes, old towns, coastal roads, or culinary highlights. The internet already has the hundredth travel report from the ten-thousandth GS rider. All I’ll say: they’re all lying. It’s even more beautiful.” The petrol group’s plan looked simple on paper: about 1,000 km from Graz to Dubrovnik, then another 1,000 km back north via Sarajevo. For Manfred, that’s where the real planning began – a second table tracking not just kilometers and riding time, but distances to the next charger. In the end, the plan held up well; the longest gap between chargers was about 225 km, comfortably within range. Day-to-day deviations came mostly from weather, ferries, road closures, and ordinary touring chaos – not from the electric bike. After the group returned through Bosnia, Manfred split off solo for another roughly 1,000 km home via Slovenia, the Großglockner, Mittersill, and several Alpine passes. Total distance: over 3,000 km. Manfred: “When planning, the others were mainly interested in two numbers: kilometers and travel time. I was interested in a third as well: “How far is the nearest power outlet?” That’s why, alongside the actual trip planning, I kept a second spreadsheet. While the petrol riders only knew where we’d sleep and drive, I also knew where my motorcycle and I would get our energy boost along the way.” On the road, the electric bike settled naturally into the ‘sweeper’ position at the back of the group – not because it was slow, but because the big adventure bikes, somewhat surprisingly, accelerated out of overtakes more gently than expected. When Manfred asked the R 1250 GS and Multistrada riders to give it more throttle on passes, the R 1250 GS rider insisted he already rode flat out – after which Manfred quietly backed off rather than risk a collision. He also highlights one underrated electric advantage: ultra-low-speed control. No clutch, no revs, no stalling – useful when the R 1300 GS routed the group onto increasingly rough, washed-out, muddy tracks better suited (on paper) to the ‘Adventure’ and ‘Enduro’ branding on the petrol bikes than to his own bike’s ‘Sports Road’ category. He couldn’t resist pointing that out to his companions; they were not amused. A city-traffic anecdote: stopped at lights beside the R 1300 GS in Sarajevo, its rider revved theatrically while waiting for green – only for the silent electric bike to pull away faster off the line, with no clutch or engine drama to manage. Another Sarajevo moment: to cut a 200-meter walk down to nothing, Manfred ‘pushed’ his powered-off-looking bike through a pedestrian zone at walking pace – technically legal, since a wheeled motorcycle counts as pedestrian traffic if no one can tell the motor is running. Overall, his companions can attest the electric bike never stood out dynamically – it stayed glued to the bike ahead even past 180 km/h. Its worst showing, ironically, came when Manfred led at the front through Bosnia and refused to exceed speed limits by more than 20 km/h – much to the group’s dismay. The widespread assumption before the trip – that petrol and electric bikes can’t tour together because the group will constantly be waiting on the electric one – turned out, in Manfred’s words, to be complete nonsense. The key factor: his bike started every morning full, while the petrol group was still checking tire pressure and weather apps over breakfast. Three to four hours of riding later, hunger stops did the charging for him; often a partial top-up during lunch was enough, and some days needed no charging stop at all. His bike supports three charging types – up to 12.3 kW via Type 2, up to 7 kW via three-phase power, and up to 3.3 kW via a standard household socket – used respectively on the road, for fun/emergency top-ups, and overnight at hotels. By the end, Manfred reckons he spent about as much time waiting for petrol riders at gas stations as they spent waiting for him at chargers. Manfred had never quite been happy with the stock Pirelli tires on his electric bike – wear was steep on the 2025 tour – so he fitted fresh Metzelers before this trip. Wear turned out excellent (only about 1.5 mm lost over 3,000+ km), but partway through Bosnia the bike started feeling odd in corners. When the group’s most vocal electric-bike skeptic, the R 1250 GS rider, borrowed it for a test ride, his verdict was blunt: great motor, terrible chassis, wobbling over bumps in lean – he’d never buy one. The real cause, discovered the next morning: a rear tire pressure of roughly 1 bar (practically flat), caused by a three-centimeter nail picked up somewhere in Dubrovnik. A Sarajevo tire shop fixed it in minutes for ten euros – plug in, air up, done – quietly clearing both the tires and the chassis of blame, and leaving Manfred crediting his small battery-powered air pump as the unsung hero of the trip. Hotels were consistently helpful about charging, most not even asking for payment (Manfred insisted on a flat 5-euro fee per night regardless). His one real complaint: charging fan noise – his “No Noise” marketed electric bike was louder overnight than all four petrol bikes combined, running its cooling fan continuously while charging. He asks manufacturers directly to fix this. Other asides: a plea to petrol riders to think about people standing behind them when they start a cold engine (especially night-train staff working around the bikes), and a tongue-in-cheek warning to Balkan snakes to watch for the Ducati Multistrada before crossing the road. A telling comparison: his electric bike used under 9 kWh per 100 km – roughly the energy content of one liter of gasoline – while the petrol bikes burned at least four liters per 100 km covering the same roads, speeds, and corners. He notes that the extra energy the four petrol bikes burned over the ~2,200 km group route could heat his daughter’s modern heat-pump house for half a winter. He closes with praise for the R 1300 GS rider’s hotel picks, especially two four-star, motorcycle-friendly properties in Sarajevo and Vransko, and a final charging/coffee stop at the R 1300 GS and F 750 GS riders’ home before the last 100 km. Asked for their verdict, the group was generally positive but flagged real trade-offs: “In the end, the charging stops didn’t slow us down because during shared breaks, we often used the available charging options. That way, we could usually continue riding together. However, the effort required to plan charging stops, search for alternatives if stations were occupied, and the limited ability to take spontaneous detours would personally take away a lot of the fun of a motorcycle trip for me.” “Ultimately, electric mobility always comes down to range. Many current models are too limited in this regard and are better suited for regional use. Your Zero really impressed me with its range of between 200–250 km. However, this requires a disciplined riding style, always keeping an eye on the remaining range. For me, riding a motorcycle is primarily an emotional experience where I want to be able to decide at any moment whether to speed up, cruise, extend the route, or take a shortcut. With the constant need to search for the next charging station, this spontaneity is partly lost, especially if the stations are occupied or even out of order.” “The only disadvantage for me personally would be the lack of spontaneity, which is a big part of what makes motorcycle riding so special. As long as you stick to the planned route with charging options, it surprisingly didn’t bother me much. I had expected that we would almost always have to split up during the midday break due to charging times. In the end, however, the lunch or sightseeing break was often long enough to fully charge the Zero so that it could reach the next destination. What did impress me was how quickly and directly the Zero puts its torque down the first time it overtakes you – you see how fast it shrinks into the distance, and it suddenly makes sense why someone would want to ride one.” “I never would have thought that riding style (speed, route planning) would have such a significant impact on range. But I also never would have thought that it would end up being so irrelevant: Even if we couldn’t ride together the entire day due to charging stops or range issues, we still almost always arrived at our destination at the same time.” Manfred didn’t expect a mixed-fleet tour through Dalmatia and Bosnia – regions with charging infrastructure still well behind Central Europe – to go this smoothly, especially since the entire route was planned for and by petrol bikes, with charging having to adapt around it rather than the reverse. The few tight moments came down to circumstances (or, in Knin, rider error) rather than any real limitation of the bike. His conclusion: petrol and electric motorcycles touring together already works far better than most riders would assume – the real differences show up in break planning, not in the riding itself. He closes half-jokingly asking readers not to rush out and buy electric bikes just yet, since being a small minority is exactly why hotels and chargers were so consistently available – a fleet of several electric bikes, or ones dependent solely on DC fast charging, would likely have forced real route changes. For this trip, though: the route worked, the team worked, the infrastructure was enough, and so was the bike. title: CRA and GS E&C Reveal Climate-Adaptive Residential Tower for Flood-Prone Seoul - Parametric Architecture
content: Subscribe to our daily newsletter on architecture and technology to stay ahead of the cureve! CRA–Carlo Ratti Associati, in collaboration with GS E&C, has unveiled a 140-meter-tall Climate-Adaptive Tower in Seoul that reimagines high-rise living through flood resilience and climate-responsive design. Elevated on slender stilts, the residential tower frees the ground below to absorb stormwater, preserve mature trees, and create new public spaces, embracing the principles of a sponge city while addressing the increasing impacts of climate change. Instead of occupying the entire site with a conventional podium, the tower lifts its residential volume above an open, permeable landscape. This approach allows stormwater to slow, infiltrate, and move naturally through the site before entering Seoul’s drainage network, reducing flood risks while supporting biodiversity. The ground plane becomes a shared public realm featuring gardens, community farming areas, tea houses, and social spaces that connect residents with nature. The project’s climate-responsive strategy extends vertically. Korean building regulations require refuge floors every 30 stories, and the design transforms these mandatory safety levels into elevated gardens where residents can gather during everyday life while remaining protected during emergencies. The building’s façade also responds to solar orientation: photovoltaic panels are integrated along the south-facing elevation to generate renewable energy, while vertical louvers on the east and west façades reduce heat gain from low-angle sunlight, improving thermal comfort throughout the year. By combining flood adaptation, renewable energy generation, urban agriculture, and public space into a single residential tower, the proposal demonstrates how high-rise architecture can actively contribute to climate resilience rather than simply withstand environmental challenges. The project continues CRA–Carlo Ratti Associati’s broader research into environmentally responsive skyscrapers, following projects such as CapitaSpring in Singapore and Jian Mu Tower in Shenzhen. title: Five-Way GS Title Fight Entering Final Four Races of Season - Sportscar365
content: Michelin Pilot Challenge shaping up for ultra-close title fight in top GS class… Just 40 points cover the top three and 190 span the top five contenders in IMSA Michelin Pilot Challenge GS coming out of Canadian Tire Motorsport Park, and it’s truly a toss-up with just four rounds to go. Nate Cicero and Robert Noaker have ascended to the GS lead with their third podium in the last four races aboard their No. 13 McCumbee McAleer Racing Ford Mustang GT4. The young chargers hold a 30-point lead over two-time race winners Michael Cooper and Moisey Uretsky in their No. 44 Ibiza Farm Motorsport McLaren Artura GT4 and 40 over Austin Krainz and Stevan McAleer in the No. 27 Auto Technic Racing BMW M4 GT4 EVO. A back-to-back pair of unlucky races for Turner Motorsport’s No. 95 BMW has dropped the early season championship leaders and WeatherTech Raceway Laguna Seca winners, Dillon Machavern and Luca Mars, to fourth and now 140 in arrears. Bryce Ward’s second tough result in the last three races – sandwiching a win at Watkins Glen International – sees him fifth and 190 back in his No. 57 Mercedes-AMG GT4. In a GS field that has averaged 31 entries per race, ranging anywhere from 29 to 35 cars, your “best worst finish” is a valuable metric to track. The No. 13 Mustang leads that stat, with a perfect six top-ten finishes from six starts. The No. 27 BMW is next best with five top-tens and an 11th. And after an 18th at Daytona, the No. 44 McLaren has ripped off five straight top-ten finishes. Quite how Cicero and Noaker kept themselves atop that chart is impressive to note after a first-lap incident at CTMP this weekend nearly derailed their race. When caught up in a multi-car skirmish at Turn 5, the No. 13 car fell from sixth on the grid to 25th, but rebounded to third at the checkered flag. One of this series’ fun quirks is that Stevan McAleer races against his own MMR team he co-founded with Chad McCumbee. McAleer’s brother Stuart is often a more omnipresent McAleer in the MMR pit box on race weekends. On Saturday, Cicero had the fun yet possibly unenviable task of trying to pass his team boss and the No. 27 car in the late stages. Last year, the battle for third in the championship flipped in the last race when McAleer, the driver, emerged ten points and one spot ahead of the MMR entry driven by Jenson Altzman for the full season with Cicero as co-driver the second half. The elder McAleer, for his part, was delighted to finally secure the Auto Technic pair’s first podium of the year – just as they did in 2025. But their run to second was not without its challenges. Combined, Turner’s No. 95 BMW and Winward’s No. 57 Mercedes-AMG have two wins and six podiums this season. But they’ll need a rally in the final four races after the month of June and start of July dealt them some unexpected tough hands. Poised for a fifth top-five in as many races, debris struck the No. 95 car in the waning stages at Watkins Glen and dropped it to an unrepresentative 17th. The trip to CTMP was no better as the No. 95 car suffered suspension damage in the aforementioned first-lap kerfuffle and fell down the order to 23rd by the finish. The No. 57 car suffered an alternator belt issue at Mid-Ohio, bounced back quickly with a win at Watkins Glen, then fell back down again with damage and a second finish outside the top 20 in three starts. These are championship-caliber teams so they’ll no doubt be back in the fight for the final few events if the luck can turn. Coincidentally, both McAleer and McCumbee McAleer Racing have a lot to look forward to next time out at Road America. MMR won at the track last year with Cicero and Altzman. McAleer won a year earlier in 2024, as part of RS1’s Porsche effort with Trent Hindman. Mars won at VIR last year with Jan Heylen in an RS1 Porsche en route to their eventual GS title. Turner and Winward’s Pilot Challenge recent histories at the upcoming venues have, like their 2026 campaigns, also been intertwined. In 2023, Winward Racing won on the track at Road America with Ward and Daniel Morad but were sent to the rear post-race for a fuel capacity infraction. Turner most recently won in GS at Road America in 2021 with Machavern and Bill Auberlen. Turner’s most recent GS win at VIR came in 2020 with Auberlen and Robby Foley, a race Winward qualified fastest with Russell Ward. Winward has a win at Indianapolis, in the venue’s one year hosting a four-hour race in 2023. But the big star of the last two venues is Ibiza Farm Motorsport, whose No. 44 McLaren went back-to-back to win at Indianapolis and Michelin Raceway Road Atlanta. Led by CEO Manuel Colon, GS Property LLC now coordinates multiple stages of the residential renovation process, including project planning, budget organization, contractor management, construction oversight, scheduling and asset repositioning. The company's evolution reflects a growing need among property owners and investors for structured project management, particularly when renovation work involves multiple vendors, changing timelines and properties located outside the owner's immediate area. "We started by doing the work ourselves and learning the business from the ground up," Colon said. "That experience gave us a clear understanding of what can go wrong during a renovation and what systems are needed to keep a project organized, accountable and moving forward." GS Property LLC initially focused on direct residential remodeling projects. As its workload increased, the company began developing internal processes that allowed it to oversee multiple projects, coordinate contractor activity and manage project requirements across different locations. That operating model has become the foundation of the company's current platform. Rather than focusing on a single construction service, GS Property LLC works to coordinate the complete execution process. The company helps clients organize project scopes, establish working budgets, evaluate contractor needs, monitor progress and address issues that arise during renovation. "Many property owners know what they want to accomplish, but they do not always have the time, local relationships or operational experience to manage every detail," Colon said. "Our role is to create structure around the project and help move it from the planning stage to completion." The company currently supports residential improvement projects in Florida, Texas and selected U.S. markets. Its clients include individual property owners, private investors, real estate groups and international clients managing properties in the United States. For owners who live outside the market where a property is located, renovation management can present additional challenges. These may include identifying contractors, monitoring expenses, reviewing project progress and responding to unexpected construction issues. GS Property LLC's project execution model is intended to provide a centralized point of coordination for those responsibilities. "When clients are not physically present, communication and accountability become even more important," Colon said. "They need accurate information, consistent oversight and a team that understands both the construction process and the investment objectives behind the property." The company's services include residential renovation management, contractor coordination, construction oversight, project scheduling and asset repositioning support. Each project is reviewed based on its condition, proposed scope of work and operational requirements. GS Property LLC said its approach is centered on practical execution rather than short-term speculation. The company evaluates renovation needs, project timing and improvement strategies with the goal of helping clients make informed decisions about their properties. "Every project is different," Colon said. "The budget, condition of the property, local market and intended use of the asset all influence the execution strategy. A successful renovation requires more than construction knowledge. It requires planning, discipline and consistent follow-through." As part of its long-term strategy, GS Property LLC is also developing a larger real estate project platform that may support future residential initiatives in the United States and Latin America. The platform remains under development. According to the company, its initial focus will be on building repeatable operating systems, strengthening project oversight and creating a framework that can support responsible growth across multiple markets. The company plans to continue expanding its contractor network, improving its project management systems and increasing its ability to coordinate residential renovation projects at scale. Colon said the company's growth has been shaped by direct industry experience, operational discipline and the ability to adapt to changing project conditions. "Real estate opportunities can look strong on paper, but the final result depends on execution," Colon said. "Our objective is to build a company that can manage the operational side of a project with clarity, consistency and accountability." GS Property LLC will continue focusing on residential remodeling, renovation management and asset improvement while further developing its project execution platform. "Our mission is to help turn real estate plans into organized, completed projects," Colon said. "We are building the systems, relationships and operational structure needed to support that mission over the long term." GS Property LLC is a real estate project execution company specializing in residential remodeling, renovation management, contractor coordination, construction oversight and asset repositioning. Led by CEO Manuel Colon, the company works with property owners, private investors and real estate organizations on residential improvement projects in Florida, Texas and selected U.S. markets. title: From Farmers Markets to Meijer Shelves: Mr. G’s Kettle Corn Pops and Grows - Meijer Newsroom
content: Here you can read all the latest Meijer corporate news and team members stories. In 2012, Greg Reece was driving a truck by day and popping kettle corn on the side to bring in a little extra cash. Once a week, he hauled his homemade recipe to a local farmers’ market, expecting a modest boost to his paycheck, not the start of a brand. But Mr. G’s Kettle Corn didn’t stay a once-a-week side hustle for long. “It just kept selling and selling every week,” Greg said. As demand climbed, he added more farmers’ markets, festivals and community events. Greg said yes to every opportunity he could manage, building the business one pop-up at a time. “We were popping popcorn out of my driveway,” he said. “That’s how I got into retail.” The growth eventually prompted Greg to trade his trucking route for the business full-time. Today, he produces thousands of pounds of popcorn each month in Louisville, Kentucky, supplying events, venues and stores across the region. Mr. G’s Kettle Corn is also served in stadiums at the University of Kentucky and Western Kentucky University. Greg also keeps his supply chain close to home, sourcing popcorn from Kentucky and partnering with local suppliers for the bags and boxes used in production. That commitment helps Mr. G’s stand out, especially for customers who want their purchase to support the community behind the product. “When you buy a bag, you’re not just supporting me,” Greg said. “You’re supporting other businesses right here in Kentucky, too.” That local roots story helped open the next opportunity: Meijer. Greg reached a milestone when he began working with the retailer through its local supplier program. It started when a Kentucky Meijer store director in his community took interest and it grew from there into a wider footprint. Today, Mr. G’s Kettle Corn is stocked in Meijer stores across Kentucky, southern Indiana and southern Ohio, with flavors including sweet-and-salty kettle corn, caramel corn and movie theater popcorn. The partnership has also increased demand, pushing Greg to think bigger about what comes next. “The volume alone at Meijer has enabled me to start looking for more equipment,” he said. Greg said he also values the communication and support that come with the partnership, including regular updates and opportunities to connect with other local vendors. © Copyright 1996-2026 Meijer, Inc.
